Brit milah. The name means covenant, and it refers to the circumcision ceremony that welcomes a newborn Jewish boy into the covenant community. The ceremony takes place on the eighth day after birth, a timing so significant that it is observed even if the eighth day falls on Shabbat or a holiday.

A trained mohel—a Jewish ritual circumciser—performs the procedure, which is followed by a blessing and a festive meal called a seudah. The ritual symbolizes the Covenant of Abraham, the foundational agreement between God and the Jewish people. Attending the brit milah is considered a valued mitzvah, a commandment and privilege, and guests are invited to witness and celebrate what is called the simchat bris, the joy of the covenant.

Traditionally, the baby receives his Hebrew name during the brit milah ceremony, and this name may differ from his secular name. A kvater, godparents, traditionally carry the baby to the ceremony, while the sandek, often called the godfather, holds the child during the procedure itself.

After the circumcision, a Hebrew blessing is recited that expresses gratitude for God's commandments and the privilege of entering the covenant. The ritual's importance means it is considered obligatory in Orthodox and Conservative Judaism, though Reform Judaism offers alternatives, including naming ceremonies without circumcision.

The brit milah establishes the baby's formal entry into the Jewish tradition. After the ceremony, the child is fully recognized as a member of the Jewish people. The brit milah is the first of several major lifecycle ceremonies in Jewish tradition, all of which mark important transitions and connections to the community.
